paragraphs.text:
Of Saint Gregory: Against Arius and Sabellius.

1. "My heart has poured forth a good word," the Psalmist was saying just now. This good Word of God the followers of Arius and Achillius, uttering the most impious of claims, have dared to proclaim a creature and a thing made, and they have drawn many into their own error. The followers of Sabellius, who think the opposite of these, try to do away with the hypostasis of the Son. They suppose that they are honoring the Father himself, who is one, under two names, and so they call him "Son-Father." These two opinions have been set like two snares by the people just named. Between them runs a middle way, narrow and hard, which leads to life, as the Gospel says. Most people turn aside from it and become the prey of one snare or the other. You, it seems to me, are afraid of falling into either, and so you flee the very way of truth, thinking that one ought not to put forward any account of God. Take care, then, that in guarding against the error of the two you do not incur the penalty of impiety. The Savior himself stands before the true way and has cried out, "I am the way and the truth." Do not turn aside to the right or to the left, so that you may fall into neither of them. And again: "I am the door of the sheep. Whoever does not enter through me, but climbs in some other way, is a thief and a robber." Such a one will be caught in a snare and will perish. So let those who have turned their minds toward either error hear this: our Savior Jesus Christ is by nature the Son of God and is called so. He is not something made that is called

"Son" by a manner of speaking, as we are. He has no beginning but is eternal, and for this reason he will also reign with the Father through the endless ages in his own hypostasis.

2. But perhaps someone might say: "Whatever is without beginning must also be unbegotten. How then could the Son rightly be called without beginning, when his very name implies a beginning? He is named Son from having been begotten, and no one would deny that being begotten falls under a beginning. If he is a Son, it is clear to us that he received a beginning from his begetting." Perhaps someone might also add [?] an end, following the philosophers' argument. For the Apostle too says that he will be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him, and that he will hand over the kingdom to the God and Father. From this it has been supposed that, since he did not exist before he was begotten, he will pass again into non-existence. Climb up with me onto the secure ground of faith, so that you are not swept away, as if by a violent gust, by the deceit of such reasonings, like chaff that the wind scatters, from the narrow and straight way into the pits of destruction. The Father of all is unbegotten and eternal, wise and powerful, and the Apostle, preaching the gospel of faith in him, proclaims to all "Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God." How then can they dare to place his begetting in time and suppose that he is neither eternal nor without beginning? For if, as some suppose, the begetting of our Savior falls within the bounds of time, then not only the Son is dishonored but also the Father, according to the Son's own words: "You know neither me nor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father." The Son is dishonored as not existing before he came to be; the Father as not having power and wisdom before the Son existed. It would follow that such people suppose the Father was not even God at one time, before the Son came to be. For how could he be God if he did not possess power and wisdom? But if the divine Scriptures have declared to us that he is God always, then we must believe that he has always had wisdom and power with him, that is, Christ.

3. I remember promising earlier to show you, as in a mirror, an image of what concerns the Father and the Son, since the things of the divine nature are not subject to human reason. When God himself speaks to us, he does not speak with the full power of his greatness. He scales his voice to human hearing, so that we may be able to take in the divine voice with our ears. In the same way he scales his unbearable and incomprehensible greatness to human sight: being God, he appeared as a man. For he emptied himself, taking the form of a slave, so that we humans might be able to behold God. We are convinced that he was not a man, yet appeared as a man, while by nature he was and is God. He confined his incomprehensible greatness within a body, and through himself, as through a mirror, he displayed [?] to us the whole

greatness of God, so that, using him as a window, we might also come to behold the Father. For he is "the image of the invisible God," as the Apostle says, and he said, "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father." In the same way, the things said in the Scriptures are suited to the measure of our hearing, and because of the weakness of language they often do not befit the Godhead. So let us contemplate him with the mind, by analogy. Just as God, confined in a body, was seen by us for the sake of our eyes, so too the language used of him, which falls short of what befits God, has been proclaimed for the sake of our ears.

4. As we said before, this Scripture shows that human language cannot contain God or what concerns him. Since no part of speech remained that could express the eternity of the Son, Scripture signifies through a preposition, as through a riddle, that he is coeval with the Father. It says, "Before the morning star I begot you," and, "Before all the hills he begets me," and before every created thing. By putting forward this part of speech, Scripture shows that he is without beginning. For "before" reaches back beyond all things, and especially when it says "before the ages" it turns our mind to what is eternal and without beginning. How, then, can one who is ever with the Father be described as Son and as begotten? Since language does not reach the things of the divine nature, I offer you an image of this: the ray that comes from the sun. And how could you not say that light is born from a lamp? Yet the sun does not come first and the ray afterward. As soon as the sun exists or has come to be, the ray also exists and has come to be. As soon as the lamp exists, the light also exists, and what the lamp gives forth is plainly given forth together with it, not after some interval of time. So too God does not come first and his wisdom afterward. As soon as the God of all exists, and he has always existed, wisdom also exists, that is, Christ. And yet, since wisdom is begotten by God, it is also rightly called the offspring of the one who brings it forth. The words "Before all the hills he begets me" show that the Savior is always being begotten by the Father for humankind. As for "Today I have begotten you": he was begotten before and is always with the Father, but Scripture, placing "today" within a portion of time, signifies that he is always being begotten for those who come to him one after another, as long as it is called "today." But when "today" comes to its end together with this world, he will no longer be begotten. Having been begotten [?] for all, and seated as judge and arbiter of all, the living and the dead, he will reign forever with the [?]

5. But we must not pass over the verse "The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works" either, so that it does not plant false reasonings in those whose minds are corrupted. When the translators turned the Hebrew Scriptures into Greek, they departed slightly from their precision

and said "He created me," whereas, if you look into it, you would find "He made me." Yet even "He created me," understood precisely, is shown to be in no way at odds with "He made me." If it had said only "The Lord created me," it would have left some people with a question. But since it added "as the beginning of his ways for his works," it would plainly be understood to say: "The Lord made me to govern his works, and entrusted to me the rule over his ways." For when did the Father acquire a beginning of his ways? When was he ever inactive? From whom did he receive the power and the activity? Not always having all things in oneself implies having received them from someone else, and then some other God older than he would have to be conceived. "Who has given to him first, that it should be repaid to him?" says Scripture. If all things are from him, then no beginning of his ways and works will ever be found; he is always active. And if all things came into being through the Son, and without him not one thing came into being, then he is plainly shown to have always had his working wisdom with him. If the Father is always working, and nothing has been worked without the Son, have they perhaps taken "being created" to mean that he was fashioned at some later point so that he might work? No: "He created me as the beginning of his ways" means "He entrusted his ways to me, so that they might be under my rule." It speaks not of a beginning in time but of a ruling authority. The apostles too say that God "made him both Lord and Christ." If "made" meant a thing made and a creature, there would be two whom he made, one Lord and the other Christ. That Christ is called king is unknown to no one. Rather, "made" signifies that two kinds of rule were entrusted to him by the Father, the lordly and the kingly, or rather one rule honored with two titles, indeed with more. So let both parties, those caught in either error, be persuaded that the Son, being always with the Father, is at once begotten and without beginning. He is without beginning because he is always with the Father, and begotten because he has the Father as the source of his being. As we said of the lamp, it is the cause of the light, yet it does not come before the light but exists at the same time. So too he will be forever and will never cease to reign, since he never began either. He shows that he has always worked together with the Father when he says, "My Father is working until now, and I am working." Now "until now" would call for a "since when" [?]. But since "since when" belongs to time, he left out "since when" and said only "until now," showing that all things have always been worked together with him. For he works until now, bringing to birth, giving life, causing growth, guiding all things, and he will never cease. Idleness does not befit God, nor will he ever grow weary of working and stop.

6. I think the Arians use as a kind of support the Gospel saying "The one who sent me is greater than I," and from it they have supposed him to be a creature and a thing made. When someone addressed him as "good teacher," he replied, "No one is good but one, God," and this has led them to suspect that the Son, being a man, received the title only by a manner of speaking. And the saying in Mark, "No one knows the day of the consummation or the hour, not even the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but the Father alone," I think leads them to suspect that the Son has come to be foreign to the Father's essence. The Sabellians, for their part, have not read with careful judgment the sayings "I and the Father are one," "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father," and "When he hands over the kingdom to the God and Father." So they have fallen into the gravest error of impiety. They think that because humanity deserted its post the Son came forth from the Father for a time, and that after setting right human offenses he departed again, sank back into the Father, and was merged with him. Have you not read, you Sabellian, this passage too of the apostolic Scripture, which stands against your opinion? Among other things it says: "According to the working of the might of his strength, which he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above every rule and authority and power and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come." Does not even the Gospel saying convince you that the Son is not temporary, but that the judgment of all in the age to come has also been entrusted to the Son? "For the Father," it says, "judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father." And elsewhere the Apostle says: "At the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven with the angels of his power, in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and on those who do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ." See how those who do not obey will pay the penalty, as he says, eternal destruction, "when he comes to be glorified in his saints." And they will pay it to the Son, whom you have supposed no longer to exist.

7. If you want to know what "When he hands over the kingdom to the God and Father" really means, it must not be hidden from you, even though you are slow to accept the truth [?]

and even though this seems to me to go against Christ's command, "Do not throw your pearls before swine." But I will imitate God and so share in good hopes, not hiding the truth even from the impious. For he sends rain alike on all, and the light of day is spread equally over the just and the unjust. When you are treated with such kindness, will you not learn the truth? Will you not lend the ears of your mind, so that you may be persuaded that nothing said in the Scriptures contradicts anything else, but that the whole is in harmony and agreement with the whole? Therefore "Then he himself will be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him" and "When he hands over the kingdom to the God and Father" must not be understood as you suppose. He was made like humanity in all things and shared its sufferings, as the prophet says: "He bears our sins and is in pain for our sake; he himself took our weaknesses and carried our diseases." For he clothed himself with flesh capable of these things. And for our sake, Scripture says, God made him sin, not because he had sinned but as though he had, so that we might be justified. He became a curse for us in order to redeem us from the curse, and he was even called accursed, choosing in his compassion to share our name. In all these things he became like humanity. He took up the very form of the slave and, as though he himself had broken the law, he put forward his own person on behalf of humanity and moved the Father to mercy, calling upon him. Since the whole of humanity had not been subjected to the Son, he too seemed and was regarded as not subjected [?], taking upon himself in the Father's sight the insubordination of the people [?]. But if ever all things are subjected to the Son (for at present we do not yet see all things subjected to him), he will say, "All things have been subjected to me." And when all things have been subjected to him, then he himself will be seen to be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him. For if all of us were Christ's, Christ too would be God's and would be subjected. But if we are not yet Christ's, neither is Christ yet God's, he who suffers for our sake. So when we all become Christ's, then Christ too will be God's, subjecting through himself to the Father all those whom he had first received from him, "so that God may be all in all." As it is, he seems in a way not to be subjected to the Father, since those for whom he has stood surety, and whose image he bears, are not yet subjected to him. But when all things have been subjected to him, then he will be seen handing over the kingdom to the God and Father. By "kingdom" we must not understand the dignity of the scepter. The Father has no need of royal dignity, as though he must take back from the Son what he had earlier granted him for temporary use, recalling it. Yet that is what you seem to me to be hinting at. In that case you are impious not only toward the Son, by doing away with his hypostasis, but also toward the Father, by declaring that at one time he was not king, having ceded the kingdom to the Son, and that he will later take it back from him because he needs the dignity. But what he will hand over to him is not the

dignity of kingship, as we said before, but those who have been ruled by him and subjected to him. Having brought forward and handed over this kingdom, he will say [?]: "This is a royal house, this a priesthood, a holy nation, a people for my own possession," and, "Here am I and the children whom God has given me." For the Father gave them to him, subjecting all the nations to him: "I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession."

8. Know also that "I and the Father are one" does not do away with the hypostasis of the Son. They are one in essence, one in dignity, one in will, one in understanding, but not one in hypostasis. It can also be shown from the Apostle that "one" does not mean one and the same hypostasis, as it is often used, for example of the one who plants and the one who waters. And the distributive word separates the hypostases: "Each will receive his own reward according to his own labor." So let it be understood that "one" does not do away with the other hypostasis. Since it has been shown that neither of these sayings is at odds with the other, and that both agree with the right faith, stop holding the views of Sabellius. Turn away from wrong thinking and do good, obeying the truth. These points alone are enough to prove to you that your views are bad.

9. And you too, Achillius, maddened like Arius, hear me. Unfortunate in faith, why have you left the straight way and driven down into the pits of dishonoring the Son, suspecting him to be a thing made and foreign to the essence of God? Are not his names alone enough to prove to you that he was begotten from the Father, since he is called the wisdom and power of God? You would surely agree that wisdom and power are not made by hands or fashioned, but are virtues of the soul and, as it were, the yield of a mind deeply rooted and growing in wisdom. If wisdom was created and fashioned at some point in time, as you said, wisdom which is older than all time and every created thing, that is, the Son, then take care that you do not seem to me to make the saying "Without him not one thing came into being" contradict your opinion. Or if you say that this wisdom was created [?], then try to show us plainly that there is some other wisdom older than this one, through which the second was fashioned. For without wisdom nothing can be fashioned. This is why wisdom is with the Father and is the firstborn of all creation: so that through it all things might be fashioned. The Son is also called Word, so that he may be shown to be begotten and not supposed to be created. For a word is born, not created; it is uttered through the mouth but set in motion from the heart. The Father bears witness

for me, saying, "My heart has poured forth a good word." The Son agrees: "I came forth from the mouth of the Most High." How could your mind bear so great a burden of audacity as to suppose him a thing made?

10. You have heard what was said earlier about the Son. Now hear also what comes next: that "was," which is in the imperfect tense, carries the meaning of eternity: "In the beginning was the Word." God's beginning is not grasped by human language. For this reason, as we said earlier, whatever part of speech Scripture has used, understand "in the beginning" as a divine beginning that is eternal. And "was" in some way signifies the same thing. "The Word" shows his hypostasis to be consubstantial with the Father. We should not think that the Son was at some time unseen, hidden in the Father, nor suppose him to be a word spoken aloud or a word held in the mind. Where must such a word exist, if not in a thought or in writing, since it has no hypostasis of its own? For these reasons John said, "And the Word was," not "in God" but "with God," ascribing to the Word its own hypostasis subsisting from the Father's essence. In the same way, so that it would not be understood as the skill of a craftsman, which has its being in someone, either in a man or in a product, he said "was with God," so that he might be understood to be God from God. Besides this, he has also received the title: "And the Word was God." Whatever is God cannot have a beginning, since otherwise it would not be God. Not only we but also the disciples of the philosophers declare this, and you ought not to have a lesser understanding of God than they do.

11. So that we might believe that he subsists as God, existing from him [?], the Father gave him a human form, confining him in flesh, in order to make the Son visible to human eyes. Now that you know he subsists as God, do not imagine the Son to be inferior or lesser because he said, "The Father who sent me is greater than I." In becoming man he had to show his own greatness through humble words. He himself said, "Let your neighbor praise you, and not your own mouth." Why should he not, in humility, show himself to be less than the Father, who is uncircumscribed and fills all things, when he himself was for a time confined in flesh and measured by human eyes? Moreover, to call the cause of one's being greater than oneself is not foreign to the truth. For if there were no God, where would wisdom be? And if there were no Father, where would the Son be? See, then, how the Son is humble everywhere and in every way, while at the same time displaying the divine greatness,

First, there is what he says to the young man who addressed him as good: "Why do you call me good? No one is good but one, God." And he was right to say so. He might have put it like this: "Young man, I have appeared to you as a man, and you called me teacher, as if I were one of the scribes, and added the word 'good.' But no man is good. That title belongs to God alone. So you were wrong to call good someone who has so far appeared to you only as a man." By saying "No one is good," no one of the kind you had in mind, he showed the man his humility. But he added "but one, God," and he and the Father are one. So in a hidden way he set out the truth along with his humility, and showed that he shares in the Father's goodness. Therefore "I and the Father are one" and "I am in the Father and the Father in me" show that he is equal to the Father. For the Son who comes from the perfect Father must himself be perfect. 12. But perhaps you will also say this: If the Father, being perfect, fills all things, what room is left for the Son, who is also perfect? My answer is that they receive and contain each other. "For I," he says, "am in the Father, and the Father is in me." And if they contain each other, they must be equal to each other in greatness. You will certainly want to hear how they can be in each other, since it seems that one must be contained by the other. What is contained is inside what contains it, but what contains cannot in turn be contained by what it contains. Do not suppose that God has an empty space inside himself in which he has received the one he contains. That is how we must think about human beings. We cannot contain others, and we cannot pass into another. And even if we could, we would contain and be contained by means of empty space. But in the case of God we must think of something like this. Two or more kinds of knowledge, such as medicine, philosophy and others, can come together in a person's soul. They do not crowd one another in the one [?] space of the soul. Though they are many, they have plenty of room and make way for one another completely. They fill the soul without pushing one another out, so that even to the most searching observers they seem to be a single substance. Yet although they are seated in one and the same mind, they differ from one another, for medicine is one thing and philosophy another. In the same way the Father and the Son occupy the same place and receive each other. They are one, as we said a little earlier, and differ from each other only in hypostasis and in name, while they are in each other. Take the scent of perfume spread through the air. The two are in the same place and seem to be mingled together, yet in truth you will find that the air is one thing and the scent another. And again, the light from the sun and the breaths of the winds,

13. No doubt you will also put this question to me: If the Father has filled all things, and the Son as well, what place is left for the opposing power? It would not be fitting for God to have his enemy alongside him. But if God [?] were not present wherever the ruler of wickedness happens to be, then God would turn out to be limited and partial. For my part, I say that God is everywhere and that there is no place where God is not, even if the ruler of wickedness happens to be somewhere. When the sun's rays fall on mud and filth, they are not soiled. Instead they make these things disappear, drying them up with their heat. In the same way "our God" is called "a consuming fire," and "Fire shall burn before him," so that he may be a lamp and a light to those he loves, but a consuming fire to his enemies. "For he will burn up his enemies round about," it says. That is why the ruler of wickedness, trying to escape God's fiery darts, runs through every place. But he finds God everywhere as he passes through the whole human race. When he finds people who are fervent in the Spirit, he flees from their burning heat too. But when he finds a refuge, swept and put in order, in someone who does not have the Spirit of God, he rests there a little while and then is destroyed along with the one who took him in. For the one who took him in will also be seen as an enemy, since he made a friend of the one who rebels against God. 14. I think this is enough by way of proof on these points too. But I must not leave the following question unaddressed, as if I had overlooked it, or as if I had sailed past it in my eagerness to reach other matters, driven along by a violent wind. How is it that, along with everyone else, not even the Son knows the day, when he has the Father in himself and is himself in the Father? This too expresses humility beyond measure. The Son of God had to humble himself beyond measure, since he had also surpassed everyone in the rest of his way of life. By saying that he did not know, he showed humility to those who heard him. But so that he would not seem to be lying, he said, "except the Father alone knows." In words he denied that he knew, but by the force of this riddle he admitted it. For if the Father alone knows, then the Son knows as well, since he and the Father are one. So from this two benefits have come [?]

to humanity: an example of humility, and ignorance of the end of the world, which is what holds life together. What could be harder to know than the day of the end, except God the Father himself? But he knew the Father, for he said, "so that you may know me, as the Father knows me and I know the Father." How then could he not know the day, which he himself also created? For without him nothing came into being. These few words have shown how the matter stands, so let it not stand in anyone's way on the road to the right faith. You followers of Sabellius and of Arius, who have gone so far apart from each other, have now come to know the whole truth from what has been said. Join me in friendship, then. Come into the middle, between the two snares, and you will find the way of truth. Walk in it, and you will see eternal life.
